memory_update.text: Track InP substrates as a high-score New Hotspots chain: AI optical demand -> indium raw material -> InP substrate growth -> export permits -> qualified six-inch substrates -> lasers/transceivers.

InP substrate growth and China-linked export permits appear to be a stronger bottleneck node than downstream mega-cap AI demand because wafer qualification and raw indium control limit substitution speed.

Track sulphur/sulphuric acid as a cross-commodity hotspot: hydrocarbon-refining byproduct -> Gulf logistics -> China acid export ban -> smelter-acid replacement supply -> copper SX-EW, HPAL nickel, fertiliser, and industrial-acid customers.
Sulphur supply has a byproduct-trap structure: downstream users cannot directly command more sulphur production if refinery byproduct output or shipping lanes are constrained.

Near-term catalysts to monitor: China sulphuric acid export-ban duration through August 2026, Hormuz shipping status, Japanese/Korean smelter-acid cargo flows, HPAL curtailments, copper acid procurement, and InP export-permit approvals.

Need primary-source verification for company-level exposure: AXTI filings on Tongmei/export permits/backlog/capex; COHR and LITE earnings-call comments on InP supply, wafer inventory, supplier qualification, and AI optical demand.

Need public-market mapping for low-attention sulphur and acid beneficiaries: smelter-acid exporters in Japan/Korea, sulphur traders/logistics operators, port assets, chemical distributors, fertiliser intermediates, and HPAL input suppliers.
Need vessel-tracking and customs-data confirmation before treating new sulphur/acid trade corridors as durable investment nodes rather than temporary emergency rerouting.

If InP substrate prices remain elevated while downstream optical companies remain sold out or capacity-constrained, the funnel should prioritize upstream substrate suppliers and qualification gates over generic AI optical names.
If China relaxes acid exports or Hormuz logistics normalize, the sulphuric-acid hotspot thesis should be downgraded unless evidence shows lasting contract repricing or customer qualification shifts.

summary: Initial Serenity Layer 2A map for 'New Hotspots': the strongest chokepoint clusters in the provided evidence are not the obvious mega-cap AI leaders, but upstream or adjacent constraint nodes: InP substrates for AI optical interconnects, sulphur/sulphuric acid for copper/nickel/fertiliser chains, and logistics/regulatory rerouting created by trade restrictions and geopolitical disruptions. Low-attention bottleneck value may hide in substrate growers, specialty optical suppliers, acid/sulphur trade routes, smelter-acid byproduct suppliers, HPAL input logistics, testing/qualification gates, and regulated export-permit dependencies.

supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI data-center bandwidth growth drives demand for high-speed optical transceivers, lasers, and photonic components, which in turn increases demand for InP wafers and qualified substrates.

China is reported to control roughly 70% of global raw indium output in the provided evidence, making upstream raw material availability and export permissions a major constraint for InP supply chains.
InP substrates are required for high-performance lasers and optical devices. Six-inch qualified substrate availability appears to be a scaling gate for downstream device makers.

supply_chain_map.node: China InP and indium export permits
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: The provided evidence says China added indium and derivatives including InP to export controls on February 4, 2025, creating permit-related shipment timing risk even for non-Chinese-listed firms with China-based production.

Downstream optical suppliers need qualified, reliable substrate supply. Supplier qualification, wafer diameter, defect density, and device compatibility can slow substitution away from China-linked capacity.
Coherent and Lumentum are cited as downstream optical-component makers affected by InP availability, with capacity expansion and sold-out conditions indicating strong pull-through demand.

The provided evidence states Lumentum is reportedly sold out through 2028 despite output expansion, implying laser capacity and input substrates may be nearer-term constraints than generic AI exposure.

The provided evidence describes sulphur as a byproduct of hydrocarbon refining, creating a 'byproduct trap': supply cannot be quickly increased just because downstream copper, nickel, battery, or fertiliser demand rises.
The provided evidence frames Hormuz disruption as a critical upstream mineral-chain risk because Middle East Gulf sulphur flows feed sulphuric acid and downstream metal-processing chains.
The provided evidence says China imposed a full sulphuric acid export ban through August 2026, removing a relief valve for Chile, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, India, Brazil, and Southeast Asian buyers.

supply_chain_map.node: Smelter-acid byproduct supply from Japan and Korea
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Indonesian HPAL and Chilean copper producers are reportedly competing for replacement sulphuric acid from Japan and Korea, creating a low-attention chokepoint around byproduct acid availability and shipping priority.

The provided evidence says Indonesian HPAL capacity imports about 75-80% of sulphur from the Middle East Gulf and that some output has already been reduced, making acid/sulphur supply a direct production constraint.

Chile is cited as a primary destination for Chinese sulphuric acid in 2026 and copper SX-EW is directly exposed to acid availability, making copper production a downstream hotspot of the sulphuric acid crunch.
Saudi Arabia and India are cited as acid destinations tied to fertiliser and industrial demand; food-security policy and fertiliser production may reinforce political urgency around acid allocation.

supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: The provided evidence says the disruption generated trade routes with little historical precedent. Freight availability, vessel tracking, port handling, and route economics may become hidden bottleneck nodes.
